hits.name: Dr. Rhonda Patrick
hits.text:
Four weeks of wall squats reduced systolic blood pressure by nearly 10 points in adults with high blood pressure.

Researchers then compared continuing three sessions weekly with reducing to two, one, or none for another month. Systolic pressure remained roughly 7 mmHg below starting levels in the once- and twice-weekly groups. Continuing three sessions weekly produced the greatest reduction of about 14 mmHg. In those who stopped completely, blood pressure moved back toward baseline.

This fits with a previous analysis of randomized trials that identified isometric exercise, which involves holding a muscle contraction, as an effective way to lower resting blood pressure.

What interests me is the practical question - how much of an exercise benefit can we preserve when we temporarily have less time? This study suggests that reducing the frequency can retain part of the benefit for up to a month.
hits.draft_en:
Rhonda Patrick shared a study where four weeks of wall squats dropped the top blood pressure number by nearly 10 points in people with high blood pressure.

Three sessions a week did best, about 14 points. Dropping to one or two a week still held about 7. Stopping altogether and it crept back up.

No gym. No gear. Just your back on a wall and your legs burning.

If your blood pressure's creeping up past 50, ask your doctor about it, then go find a wall.

hits.name: Dr Shawn Baker 🥩
hits.text:
In February 2021, while in the Democratic Republic of the Congo with researchers tracking endangered bonobos, Ashley Judd was walking in the rainforest in low light when she tripped over a fallen tree. 

The impact shattered her plant based tibia in multiple places—described in contemporary accounts as a catastrophic break that put the leg at immediate risk. She spent roughly 55 hours being carried out of the remote jungle by local teams before reaching advanced care. 

Recovery involved surgery, prolonged immobilization, and extensive rehabilitation. Months later she shared video of herself walking again, emphasizing the near-loss of the limb and the role of the people who extracted her. 

In 2022, after the death of her mother Naomi Judd, she once again sustained a second, less severe fracture to the other leg. She publicly attributed it to a “freak accident” tied to grief-related clumsiness rather than any high-impact event. That break healed more quickly, and she has since discussed functional training as part of returning to activity. 

Judd is a longtime animal-rights and conservation advocate; the Congo trip itself was research-related.

Numerous scientific papers have now shown that plant based, and particularly vegan diet are associated with much higher rates of fracture.  Whether this was the underlying reason for her fractures is hard to say for sure, but undoubtedly one has to wonder if eating a diet based on emotion is a good idea.
hits.draft_en:
Shawn Baker posted the story of Ashley Judd shattering her tibia after tripping in the Congo, then breaking the other leg the next year. He links it to her plant-based diet.

Whatever you make of that, the bigger point stands for anyone over 50: bones get weaker if you don't look after them.

Enough protein. Enough calcium. And heavy things lifted regularly, because loading your bones is what tells them to stay strong.

A fall at 30 is a bruise. At 60 it can be a broken hip.

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD
hits.text:
Saturated fat was supposed to clog your arteries. A brand new randomized trial just put that to the test.

Researchers in Norway assigned 193 adults with obesity to one of three diets for up to 2 years. One was low-carb with about 30% of energy from saturated fat. That's 3 times the 10% cap in the Dietary Guidelines. The other two were higher-carb, guideline-style diets.

On the high saturated fat diet, triglycerides dropped 20 to 35% and HDL rose 5 to 18%. On the higher-carb diets those stayed fairly flat.

LDL went up 5 to 10%, mostly the large, buoyant particles. ApoB did not go up significantly. Small dense LDL did not go up significantly. And CT scans at 12 months showed no difference in coronary artery calcium between the diets.

The lead researcher said the study "challenges the contention that a higher intake of saturated fat has an inherent negative impact of overall disease risk."

The Study and my video below...
hits.draft_en:
Ken Berry shared a new Norwegian trial: 193 adults with obesity were put on a low-carb diet with about 30% of energy from saturated fat, or on higher-carb guideline-style diets, for up to two years.

On the high-saturated-fat diet, triglycerides fell 20 to 35% and HDL rose. LDL went up 5 to 10%, but ApoB and small dense LDL didn't rise significantly, and heart scans at 12 months showed no difference in artery calcium.

One trial doesn't settle it. But it's another reason to stop fearing real food and look at the full blood picture.

When a person loses fat, their fat cells shrink, but the number of fat cells stays the same. The number is largely set during childhood and adolescence, and it holds steady through adulthood in lean and obese people alike, even after major weight loss.

That doesn't mean the cells never change. About 10 percent of fat cells are replaced every year, and the body keeps the total number steady.

This is why I care so much about what kids eat, and it's why I focus adults on fat cell size. Smaller, healthier fat cells are the goal, and that comes from lowering insulin and keeping the weight off over time.

The Forest Laws Never Ended

After 1066, William the Conqueror and the Norman kings turned vast stretches of England into royal forest. Inside those bounds the red deer and fallow deer belonged to the crown. 

A peasant who killed one to feed his family could lose his eyes, his hands, his manhood, or his life. The laws were written so that, as one chronicler put it, the English would have “nothing but their eyes to weep with.”

The meat of the wild was reserved for the ruling class. Everyone else was expected to live on what the land under the plow could produce: grain, pottage, the occasional chicken or pig if they were lucky. When the Charter of the Forest finally arrived in 1217 it removed the worst mutilations and the death penalty, but the underlying idea stayed intact: the best animal protein was a privilege, not a right.

That idea never really died. It simply changed costume.
Today the same hierarchy reappears in softer language. Elite tables still feature steak, lamb, and game. Private jets still carry foie gras and dry-aged beef to conferences where the speakers tell everyone else that livestock are the problem. 

The recommended diet for the rest of the population is heavy on “whole” grains, legumes, and plant protein—foods that historically filled the peasant bowl while the lords kept the animals. The rhetoric is climate, health, or equity. The practical result is the same as the old forest law: the high-quality meat stays upstream.

The punishments are no longer blinding and castration. They are subsidies, guidelines, school menus, and social pressure. But the direction of the flow has not changed. The deer still belongs to the people who write the rules. The rest are told the grain is good for them.

Mr. Horace Langley arrived in a state of what the intake form called “nervous dyspepsia and moral debility.” He had eaten beefsteak the week before. That, the nurse informed him while confiscating his trunk of clothing, was almost certainly the root of the problem.

Red meat, he was instructed, produced toxins that inflamed the system, clouded the mind, and excited the lower passions. The yogurt, by contrast, was pure.

Lunch was zwieback, stewed prunes, and a nut cream that tasted faintly of sawdust. When he asked about the steak the other patients whispered about in the night, he was given a pamphlet titled “The Poison in the Pot.”
In the afternoon came the electric light bath. He sat naked under banks of bulbs until he sweated freely, then was plunged into a cold shower while an attendant checked his pulse and noted “improved elimination.” That evening another enema. The nurse remarked that men who had previously lived on chops and roasts often required several weeks of this regimen before the craving for flesh subsided and the bowels regained their natural tone.
Langley lasted nine days. On the tenth he slipped out after breakfast, found a diner two blocks from the sanitarium, and ordered a rare sirloin. He ate it slowly, then walked to the station. He described it as a thick, rubbery, greenish film of mucus, undigested food, and toxins coating the intestines of almost everyone who ate “normal” food. The only way to get rid of it, he said, was his special cleanse kits—herbs, bentonite clay, and fiber blends sold under names like Arise and Shine. 

The idea traveled fast through raw-food and vegan circles. It slotted neatly into older “mucusless diet” teachings: animal products and cooked food supposedly left behind a toxic residue that pure fruit, fasting, or aggressive cleansing would finally purge. Forums filled with before-and-after photos of long, ropey strands people had passed. Each strand was treated as proof that years of “impure” eating had been coating their insides. 

Some people cycled through cleanse after cleanse, chasing the feeling of finally being empty and pure. 
Pathologists who had examined thousands of intestinal specimens never saw anything matching the description. 

Gastroenterologists called it a fabrication. Even some long-term raw vegans and fasting clinicians eventually pushed back, pointing out that the dramatic ropes usually appeared only after people swallowed the very ingredients that swell into gelatinous casts—clay, psyllium, and stimulant herbs. The “plaque” was, in most cases, the cleanse itself. 

The marketing worked anyway. It gave people a tangible enemy inside their bodies and a product that promised to defeat it. For a while, in certain corners of the wellness world, the goal wasn’t just to eat plants. It was to keep cleaning until the last invisible layer was gone—even if the layer had never been there to begin with.

The Cochrane review that quietly undercuts the fruit-and-vegetable miracle story
In 2013, a team of researchers set out to answer a simple question: if you get people to eat more fruits and vegetables, does it actually prevent heart attacks, strokes, or early death? They turned to the Cochrane Collaboration, the gold standard for systematic reviews of randomized trials, and looked only at studies designed for the primary prevention of cardiovascular disease.

What they found was almost nothing.
Ten trials, just 1,730 people total. Some gave people fruit or vegetables (usually a single type). Others simply told them to eat more. Follow-up was short—weeks to a few months at most. Not a single trial reported a heart attack, stroke, cancer diagnosis, or death. The studies were too brief and too small to measure those outcomes. The authors stated it plainly: none of the trials were long enough to examine effects on cardiovascular events.

What the trials did measure were intermediate markers. Advice to eat more produce produced a modest drop in systolic blood pressure of about 3 mmHg, based on just two trials. Giving people the food itself showed no clear benefit on blood pressure or cholesterol. Side effects were minor and unremarkable.

The review’s conclusion was restrained but unmistakable: there is very little evidence from randomized trials that simply increasing fruit and vegetable intake, without other dietary or lifestyle changes, prevents cardiovascular disease. More trials are needed.

That is the entire hard-outcome story from the highest-quality evidence available. No data on longevity. No data on cancer. No data on actual heart attacks or strokes. The large reductions in disease and death that are routinely attributed to “5 a day” come from observational studies, not from the randomized experiments that can isolate cause and effect.

The Cochrane review remains one of the clearest statements in the literature: when you demand the kind of evidence that matters for hard clinical outcomes, the fruit-and-vegetable prescription has almost none.

The King of Chefs Who Built Empires on Butter and Cream

In the glittering salons of Napoleonic Paris, one man turned sauce into strategy. Marie-Antoine Carême, the abandoned street child who became “the king of chefs and the chef of kings,” did not merely cook for the powerful—he rewrote the rules of French cooking around fat. 

Working for Talleyrand, the diplomat who used banquets as weapons, Carême created the mother sauces that still define haute cuisine: béchamel, velouté, espagnole, and allemande. These were not delicate broths. They began with butter-and-flour roux, simmered in rich stocks, and finished with heavy cream, egg yolks, and more butter. Allemande was a velouté enriched with cream and yolks until it shone. Béchamel was milk thickened with butter, then often enriched further. Dishes arrived at the table swimming in velvet sauces that carried flavor the way architecture carries weight—Carême himself compared pastry to architecture, and his sauces were the load-bearing walls.

Napoleon commissioned him for the wedding cake of his marriage to Marie-Louise; Talleyrand relied on him to soften foreign dignitaries. The food was unapologetically rich. Butter was not a garnish. It was the medium.

Decades later, epidemiologists noticed something that still confounds simple diet rules: the French Paradox. Populations that ate substantial amounts of saturated fat from butter, cream, and cheese showed lower rates of coronary heart disease than expected compared with other countries consuming similar levels of animal fat. 

Traditional French cooking, the kind Carême codified, was built on those same fats. Observational data from the late 20th century repeatedly showed France with relatively low CHD mortality despite high dairy-fat intake. Portion size, meal structure, and lifestyle played roles, but the core observation held: heavy use of butter and cream in classical French cuisine did not produce the heart-disease epidemic the fat-heart hypothesis predicted.

Carême died at 49, likely from years over charcoal stoves, but the sauces he systematized outlived him. They remain a living argument that the fats of traditional French cooking were not the villains later theory made them out to be.

The hormone scare about regular beef falls apart once you see the actual numbers.

The difference between implanted and non-implanted beef is less than one nanogram. Why? Read on...

A 3-ounce serving of beef from an implanted steer has 1.9 nanograms of estradiol. Beef from a non-implanted calf has 1.3 nanograms. That is a difference of 0.6 nanograms.

The University of Nebraska puts that next to a child's body, which makes around 50,000 nanograms of estrogen per day. Their same page lists 340 nanograms of estrogen in peas and 2,000 in cabbage.

Buy the beef you can afford. Regular grocery store beef is still a health food.

We're giving out meat sticks this year!
I called candy slow poison two Halloweens ago. The label on a fun-size Snickers backs me up.

Three of those little bars nearly use up a child's whole day of added sugar. Why? Read on...

One fun-size Snickers has 8 grams of added sugar. Three of them is 24 grams. The American Heart Association says children should get no more than 25 grams of added sugar a day, and children under 2 should get none at all.

That 25 grams is supposed to cover the cereal, the juice and the snacks too. And very few kids come home with three pieces.

The AHA's own statement says the links between added sugar and heart risk factors in kids show up "at levels far below current consumption levels." It ties added sugar in children to more body fat and worse blood lipids.

Let them dress up and have fun. Feed them meat and eggs before they go out, and read the labels on what comes home.

hits.name: Ken D Berry MD
hits.text:
Are you tired of the "Orange Juice is Magically Healthy" argument? I know I am.
Almost everything you eat or drink changes gene activity in your blood cells. A cup of coffee does it. A steak does it. A donut does it. A workout or a bad night's sleep does it. So when someone tells you orange juice "alters gene expression," they haven't told you anything that makes it good for you.

Sounds great if you don't know better, but it is meaningless!

This post is circulating that says 500 mL of orange juice a day changes genes for inflammation, blood pressure and metabolism, and that this could help diabetes, obesity, hypertension, stroke and heart disease. Why is that misleading? Read on...

The paper is Fraga et al. in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, 2025. Twenty healthy adults, ages 21 to 36, drank 500 mL of orange juice every day for 60 days. There was no control group and no placebo. Nobody in that group had diabetes! 

The main finding was that gene activity in white blood cells changed, which is exactly what you'd expect from drinking almost anything every day for two months. That is not a blood sugar result, not a weight result, and not a blood pressure result from this paper.

That 500 mL glass of OJ carries about 42 grams of sugar and almost no fiber, per USDA data. Your liver still has to handle that fructose load every single day.

When you look at real outcomes instead of gene charts, fruit juice looks bad, really bad. 

Muraki et al. followed three large U.S. cohorts and found every three extra servings of fruit juice a week tied to an 8% higher type 2 diabetes risk. Imamura et al. pooled 17 cohorts and found each extra daily serving of fruit juice tied to a 7% higher type 2 diabetes incidence after adjusting for body fat.

Orange juice is still sugar water with a vitamin C sprinkle and a flavor packet. A gene chart from 20 people with no control group is meaningless.

Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. 
https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD
